messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] K-multiv
messages.body_plain:
Borja,

the randomizations to assess phylogenetic signal using K evaluate whether there is, or not, an association between (multivariate, in the generalization of the method) phenotype and phylogeny under a BM process, where the expected value of K=1. These randomizations do NOT assess the hypothesis of K=1 or K=0 or any other value, or deviations from it. And K=0 does not mean absence of phylogenetic signal, but rather a strong deviation from what phenotypic variation would look like under BM.

A detailed treatment about the original implementation of the method, null hypotheses tested and the meaning of values of K can be found in Blomberg SP, Garland T, Ives AR. 2003. Testing for phylogenetic signal in comparative data: behavioral traits are more labile. Evolution, 57:717-745, but read also the paper on the multivariate generalization into detail (Adams, D.C. 2014. A generalized K statistic for estimating phylogenetic signal from shape and other high-dimensional multivariate data. Systematic Biology. 63:685-697.). I think both will help you with interpretingthe values you are getting.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Interpreting results of PCA
messages.body_plain:
Katey,

I’m not sure what I am about too propose is appropriate, but you could use the loadings I mentioned to find the portion of each landmark’s contribution to the overall squared PC vector length.  For example, with 2D landmarks:

PCA <- plotTangentSpace(shapedata)

P1 <- t(matrix(PCA$rotation[,1], 2, )) # change 2 to 3 for 3D
diag(tcrossprod(P1))/sum(diag(tcrossprod(P1))) # relative portions along PC 1

P2 <- t(matrix(PCA$rotation[,2], 2, )) # change 2 to 3 for 3D
diag(tcrossprod(P2))/sum(diag(tcrossprod(P2))) # relative portions along PC 2

The largest values are those for landmarks that change the most along each PC.  Keep in mind though that landmarks are not independent.  If you have a few clustered together in your configuration, they might seem small in their contributions but their collective correlated contributions have a strong influence on PC1.  In my opinion, deformation grids via TPS are a better way to visualize which landmarks are “important”.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Katey,

just to add to Mike´s comment, I think what you are looking for is the last option Mike suggested. In the list returned by plotTangentSpace, you have a component called $shapes which provides the shapes corresponding to the extremes of each of the PC axes. You can use plotRefToTarget with e.g. minPC1 and maxPC1 to obtain plots that summarize shape variation across PC1 etc. Those deformation grids allow you to interpret biologically what varies the most in your shape sample.

Hope this helps,

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Angel,

I don’t understand the statement “the semi-landmarks alignment is closely related to the rotation step of GPA”. The sliding of semilandmarks is in fact an additional step embedded within an ‘extended’ GPA algorithm. With fixed landmarks only, one translates, scales, and rotates. A mean shape is found, and the process is repeated against the mean, and this is iterated until convergence. For GPA with sliding landmarks, the algorithm includes translation, scaling, rotation and sliding. This is then iterated numerous times.

If one wishes to implement only components of this, one needs to write their own algorithm for it, or adapt an existing one.  Note however that in these cases, this results in major differences in the expected data space that results. Rohlf had a paper in the 1990s describing the different dataspaces from translation only, translation and scaling, translation, rotation scaling, etc. Each has consequences, not just as ‘a procedure’, but also in terms of what one expects in terms of patterns in data. Statistical shape theory is only valid for fully superimposed shapes: it does not apply to data in say, form space, pre-shape spaces, ‘fibers’ in pre-shape space, etc.

Dean

Testing for phylogenetic signal in comparative data: behavioral traits are more labile. Evolution, 57:717-745, but read also the paper on the multivariate generalization into detail (Adams, D.C. 2014. I appreciate any help.

Julian

Hey Dean,

Thanks for this, and the rest of your very comprehensive answers to my (many) questions :-)

Cheers,

On 16 March 2018 at 22:21, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

> Sam,
>
>
>
> “The allometry-free PCA returned PC1 explaining 60.3% of the variation, and PC2 explaining 13.9% of the variation. None of which correlate with any of my variables. The shape change also changes little between my PCA with allometry, and PCA without allometry (see attached). If allometry was supposed to account for most of my variation in PC1, then I would expect a larger difference after the removal of allometry in my second PCA plot as well, which makes me think that the variation in PC1 was not due to allometry, or, I have made a mistake along the process. “
>
>
>
> The a priori intuition in your statement above is misguided. There is no reason that allometry must account for most variation in any dataset, nor that it align perfectly with PC1.  PCA does not ‘find’ a particular biological factor; it merely rotates data to the direction of maximal variation. That direction could associate with allometry, group differences, elevation, or NOTHING. Thus any expectation that PC1 ‘shows’ some biological factor should be avoided. It is a rotation-based visualization tool, not factor exploration (for the latter try factor analysis).
>
>
>
> Second, while it is unclear what you mean by ‘expect a larger difference after the removal of allometry’, remember that the 2 PCAs are performed on different datasets (original and size-residuals). Your question implies that comparing the percentage of variation across axes across analyses is useful and meaningful. It is not, because these are based on datasets containing differing totals of variation (by definition the size-residuals have less variation than the original data). There is simply no way of knowing what percentage of variation will be on PC1, PC2 or any axis when comparing them. I know of no statistical theory that would generate any expectation in this regard, as the pattern of variation and covariation in the second dataset is conditioned on size while the former is not.
>
>
>
> The PCA analyses know nothing about other sources of variation, so it is unclear how one could derive an expectation of % variation across PC axes without the biologist having that knowledge to establish it.
>
>
>
> Dean

>
>
> I'm having some trouble in understanding the variation from my PCAs before and after the removal of allometry, which I'm hoping someone might be able to enlighten me where I am going wrong...
>
>
>
> I have a single population with 89 offspring from 7 females, and I want to test whether offspring size (whole body) effects offspring head shape. I know individual size can often be used as an allometric measure, so I tested to see whether there was a correlation between Csize and offspring size, but there was not so will keep offspring size as one of my variables.
>
>
>
> My PCA plot shows that PC1 explains 59% variation, and PC2 explains 14.5% of the variation. To check the loadings of each of my variables on each PC axis I ended up using linear models since I could not find this information in $rotation. Is there a better way than this? PC1 was significantly correlated with Csize (effect size of 3.673 sd) and PC2 was significantly correlated with size (effect size 5.103 sd).
>
>
>
> Following this discussion closely (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/geomorph-r-package/1jXm_6dNE3A), my slopes were not biologically significant and I went ahead and obtained allometry-free shapes:
>
>
>
> charrAllom <- procD.allometry(shape ~ Csize, ~ female, logsz = TRUE, data = gdf.symm, iter = 999)
>
> charrAnova <- procD.lm(charrAllom$formula, data = charrAllom$data, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE)
>
> shape.resid <- arrayspecs(charrAnova$residuals, p = dim(gdf.symm$shape)[1], k = dim(gdf.symm$shape)[2]) # allometry adjusted residuals
>
> # allometry free shapes
>
> mean.shape <- mshape(gdf.symm$shape)
>
> adj.shape <- shape.resid + array(mean.shape, dim(shape.resid))  # allometry-free shapes
>
> PCA_noAllom <- plotTangentSpace(adj.shape, axis1 = 1, axis2 = 2, groups = gdf.symm$female)# PCA of allometry-free shape
>
>
>
> The allometry-free PCA returned PC1 explaining 60.3% of the variation, and PC2 explaining 13.9% of the variation. None of which correlate with any of my variables. The shape change also changes little between my PCA with allometry, and PCA without allometry (see attached). If allometry was supposed to account for most of my variation in PC1, then I would expect a larger difference after the removal of allometry in my second PCA plot as well, which makes me think that the variation in PC1 was not due to allometry, or, I have made a mistake along the process.
>
>
>
> Thanks in advance.
>

>
> Sam

Julien,

You want to use advanced.procD.lm for this. Your design is a MANCOVA, where you have Y ~ size + group + size:group.  This last term, the interaction, is the HOS test (homogeneity of slopes). If this term is significant it implies the slopes of your groups are not the same.  At that point,  your comparisons of groups is about the slopes or lengths of the regressions, not the LS means.  See the help pages for advanced.procD.lm for examples.

Julian,

nested.update is intended to work with procD.lm objects, not advanced.procD.lm objects.  There is no reason to do an update because you have defined precisely the two models you are comparing.  nested.update is intended for models with multiple terms, hence multiple model comparisons, to make sure that fixed factor effects are compared to random effects instead of model error.

There is no reason to use nested.update on the results from advanced.procD.lm.

Mike

messages.subject: Plotting after object symmetry
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

After performing superimposition on my data, my plots look fine. But then after conducting bilat.symmetry, the plots are being reflected (i.e. pointing specimens pointing to the right and not to the left as it should be) even when I have specified 'object.sym = TRUE', as well as giving 'land.pairs'. However, some populations work with no problem (i.e. all specimens remain pointing to the left), and I use exactly the same code. I also find no real differences between my TPS files and classifier files between populations. The land.pairs are the same for all populations also. Does anyone know what else might be causing this?

I checked the following post by Jeremy who seemed to have a similar problem and was resolved by performing GPA across all populations at the same time:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/geomorph-r-package/left$20and$20right%7Csort:date/geomorph-r-package/xt8XB1nQ1uo/JVBOai7TBQAJ

But I do perform a GPA over all my populations (which I will use in another paper) and then I subset one population from this (to use in a separate paper) so that they will be comparable later on down the line.

...seems like quite a simple problem but I can't get past it.

Thanks, as always,
Sam

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = gpa.res.before$coords,
                           ind = as.factor(classifierBefore$ID),
                           size = as.numeric(as.character(classifierBefore$size)),
                           female = as.factor(classifierBefore$female))

land.pairs_left <- matrix(c( 6, 11,10,12,13,16,17,35:28,36:43,71:62))
land.pairs_right <- matrix(c(7, 8, 9, 15,14,19,18,20:27,51:44,52:61))
land.pairs <- cbind(land.pairs_left, land.pairs_right) # also tried combining right first, then left. No difference

# object symmetry using the shape output performed from gpagen (as this includes semilandmarks)
lands.objSym.H <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, replicate = ind,
                                 object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = land.pairs,
                                 RRPP = TRUE, iter = 500, data = gdf)

plot(lands.objSym.H, warpgrids = TRUE)
